description: We are a team of curious students passionate about space, science, technology, and innovation. We aim to use NASA’s open data, AI/ML, and data science to develop creative solutions to real-world challenges. We value teamwork, creativity, and hands-on learning, and welcome members skilled in programming, research, data analysis, UI/UX design, or presentation. Together, we hope to explore new ideas, learn, and build impactful solutions.
summary:
Summary:
Earth Jukebox is a browser-based studio that turns real NASA Earth data into music, so climate change can be heard as well as seen. Maps and charts leave out people who cannot rely on visuals, and slow change over decades is hard to feel on a line chart. Sound compresses time: users can hear 40 years of warming in about 20 seconds.

The app fetches live data from the NASA POWER API, computes anomalies against a 1991–2020 baseline, and maps them to pentatonic notes using the Web Audio API. Warmer years sound higher; larger jumps add more notes. Three modes are offered: Climate, Water Cycle, and Earth Symphony. A compare feature plays two places in the left and right ears on one shared pitch scale. For example, the Arctic is heard against Bengaluru.

A chart playhead and a NASA GIBS satellite map move in sync with the sound. Keyboard and screen-reader support, a written and spoken summary, a data table and .wav export make the data accessible to blind and low-vision users.
details:
Project Details:

What it does

Earth Jukebox lets anyone pick a place on a NASA satellite map and listen to its climate data. It offers three modes:

- Climate: a place's annual temperature anomaly since 1985, played in about 20 seconds. Higher note = warmer than average; a bigger jump = more notes; a tick marks each decade.

- Water Cycle: the last 60 days of rain, humidity and sunlight. Rain becomes droplets and patter, humidity sets the pad pitch, and sunlight sets brightness. Sea surface temperature is shown as a map layer.

- Earth Symphony: temperature, wind, rain, sun and humidity layered together. Temperature is the melody, wind the rhythm, rain the droplets, and sun the brightness.

Compare mode plays Location A in the left ear and Location B in the right, on one shared scale, so a faster-warming place literally sounds higher. A one-click demo compares the Arctic with Bengaluru over 40 years.

How it works

1. Fetch: data comes from the NASA POWER API (no key needed), as annual temperature since 1985 or daily data for the last 60 days.

2. Normalize: values become anomalies against the 1991–2020 average, on one shared scale so two places can be compared by ear.

3. Map to sound: values become pentatonic notes through the Web Audio API, proportional to the data, so the result stays musical rather than noisy.

4. Synchronize: a chart playhead and the map move with the sound.

Numbers come from NASA POWER. Imagery (true colour, land and sea surface temperature, precipitation, aerosols) comes from NASA GIBS.

Accessibility

Keyboard and screen-reader support; a written summary, data table and spoken summary; "Hear the scale" guide; speed control and scrubbing; no autoplay; .wav export of any soundscape.

Trust and honesty

The app is static HTML/CSS/JS with no server and no API key. Units, dates and sources are shown on screen. It never invents data, and it shows a clearly labelled cache if NASA services are down. It uses a Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity. We state its limits: results are local, not a global climate signal; POWER data is gridded and a few days behind, not live sensors; GIBS map pixels are visual context, not the data being sonified. This is an independent educational prototype, not an official NASA product.

Tools used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Audio API, NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS. [Add any libraries you used, e.g. charting or map libraries.]

Why it is creative and why it matters

It turns decades of slow change into something you can feel in seconds, and it lets blind and low-vision users explore the same data as everyone else. The left-ear/right-ear comparison makes regional differences in warming immediately audible.

Next steps

Frame-by-frame playback over GIBS imagery, sonifying numeric ocean data, more datasets and regions, narrated tours, saved soundscapes, and co-design with blind and low-vision users.
